title: Brand Protection on MercadoLibre: Latin America 2026
summary: Enforce IP rights on MercadoLibre in September 2026 with country-level trademarks, BPP filings, and SKU-level detection across Latin America.
body_markdown:
Brand protection on MercadoLibre is more complex than a single takedown program. One trademark registration does not cover every country in the region, gray market sellers are not technically violating IP law, and the infringers most likely to damage your brand are the ones who copy your product images while stripping your brand name from the listing entirely. If your current approach stops at filing complaints when you spot something, there is a lot more ground to cover.


‍


**TLDR:**


‍


- Nearly 47% of Latin Americans buy on MercadoLibre, making it the region's highest-risk marketplace for infringing listings.
- Register your trademark country-by-country before entering each market; a Mexican registration cannot support a complaint filed in Argentina.
- MercadoLibre's free Brand Protection Program (BPP) removes listings in 24-48 hours, but suspended sellers can re-register under a new account.
- Gray market cases fall outside the BPP's IP framework entirely; enforcement runs on pricing surveillance and distribution agreement tracks, not takedown tools.
- Keyword-only monitoring misses infringers who strip your mark from titles while copying your product imagery and specifications.
- MarqVision covers MercadoLibre storefronts across seven Latin American countries with SKU-level detection that catches mark-stripped listings the BPP misses.


‍


‍


## The Counterfeit Environment on MercadoLibre


E-commerce in Latin America reached[US$769 billion in 2025](https://paymentscmi.com/latin-america-ecommerce-blueprint-market-data/) , and much of that spend runs through MercadoLibre, which operates the region's most widely used commerce and fintech systems across Mercado Libre, Mercado Shops, Mercado Pago, and Mercado Envios. Nearly[47% of regional residents buy there](https://brand-monitor.com/blog/mercado-libre-how-to-protect-your-brand/) .


‍


That reach expands the surface for infringing listings. Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina draw the most complaints, concentrated in consumer electronics, apparel, footwear, and cosmetics.


‍


‍


For context, counterfeit goods accounted for an estimated $467 billion in global trade in 2021, per the[OECD trade in counterfeit goods](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/press-releases/2025/05/global-trade-in-fake-goods-reached-USD-467-billion-posing-risks-to-consumer-safety-and-compromising-intellectual-property.html) report.


‍


‍


## Types of IP Infringement Found on MercadoLibre


MercadoLibre's Brand Protection Program covers[trademarks, designs, patents, and copyrights](https://global-selling.mercadolibre.com/brandprotection/enforcement) . Each maps to a distinct enforcement problem.


‍


Trademark counterfeiting deliberately copies a registered mark, logo, or brand name to pass fakes off as genuine. It sits alongside copyright infringement as the most frequent violation you will file, with copyright cases usually involving sellers lifting your official product photography.


‍


Design copying works differently. A dupe copies the silhouette, packaging, or trade dress without using your brand name or logo. Because no trademark is involved, a registered industrial design right is the correct basis for a takedown, not a trademark claim.


‍


Gray market resellers are a different problem. The goods they sell are genuine, but they source and distribute outside your authorized channels, which means they break your contracts and undercut your pricing controls without technically violating IP law.


‍


The harder pattern to catch: infringers strip trademark use from titles and descriptions while copying your images and specifications, evading keyword and logo-based detection. This is a core challenge in[digital brand protection for global brands](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/digital-brand-protection-strategies-global-brands) .


‍


Infringement Type What It Involves Enforcement Basis Key Limitation


Trademark counterfeiting Copies your registered mark, logo, or brand name to pass fakes off as genuine Trademark registration + BPP takedown Sellers can re-register under a new account after suspension

‍


‍


## Trademark Registration Across Latin America


Registration is the structural gate for MercadoLibre enforcement, because you must enroll your rights for each country you want to report in. A mark registered in Mexico does nothing for a complaint filed in Argentina.


‍


Every Latin American jurisdiction runs on a first-to-file system, with its own opposition periods, classifications, and renewal rules. Brazil grants rights to whoever files first with INPI, regardless of prior use.


‍


File ahead of expansion. Enter a market before registering and a squatter can claim your mark first, leaving you with no basis to enforce. Similar dynamics apply when you[enforce IP rights on Alibaba](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/is-alibaba-safe-for-brands-enforce-ip-rights) , where cross-border supply chains complicate matters further.


‍


‍


## MercadoLibre's Brand Protection Program


MELI launched its Brand Protection Program over 20 years ago, in early 2000. Available in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, the reporting tool comes at no cost and covers your entire IP portfolio across all MELI platforms.


‍


On Mercado Pago, you can also protect trademarks and related rights covering illegal transmissions and devices. Any rights holder or agent can join.


‍


The program is not purely reactive. MELI applies machine learning that combines multiple variables to take proactive measures, so consistent reporting sharpens detection over time. Choosing the right[brand protection software](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/brand-protection-software) can further amplify these automated signals.


‍


‍


## How to Enroll in the Brand Protection Program


Enrollment starts with your rights documentation, and what MELI requires depends on the type of right you register. For a trademark, you attach a copy of the registration certificate issued by the trademark office of the corresponding country.


‍


If an agent files on your behalf, attach a current power of attorney granted by the rights holder.


‍


A few practical points for setup:


‍


- Enroll rights separately for each country you intend to report in, all managed under one account.
- Create multiple team profiles under that account so several people can file.
- Work in Spanish, Portuguese, or English.


‍


Reports are generally processed within 24 to 48 hours, though[brand takedown timelines](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/actual-brand-takedown-times) vary widely across platforms and regions.


‍


‍


## Filing a Complaint: The Notice and Takedown Process


Once you identify an infringing listing, you file through the program and[the listing is paused pending seller notice](https://global-selling.mercadolibre.com/devsite/manage-questions-answers-global-selling/what-is-the-brand-protection-program) , who gets a window to prove the listing does not infringe.


‍


That window is short. If the seller does not reply within four days, the listing is automatically removed.


‍


When a counter-notice arrives, review the seller's claim. Confirm the infringement and the listing is permanently removed, after which MELI reevaluates the seller for sanctions like a warning or temporary suspension.


‍


For volume, report listings individually or in bulk, and save your search criteria so monitoring teams reuse the same parameters instead of rebuilding them each sweep.


‍


‍


## How MercadoLibre Sanctions Repeat Offenders


Sanctions escalate with repetition. A confirmed claim triggers reevaluation of the seller, starting with a warning notice and temporary account suspension. Persistent infringers lose their accounts permanently.


‍


Each confirmed report compounds your position. MELI learns from accumulated BPP reports to detect infringement patterns and cancel listings proactively, so a documented history of confirmed claims strengthens both the sanction case against a seller and the automated detection over time.


‍


The ceiling: a suspended seller can re-register under a fresh account, so the deterrent value of persistent reporting only holds when you keep it up.


‍


‍


## Gray Market and Unauthorized Sellers on MercadoLibre


Gray market cases sit outside the IP framework the BPP relies on. Reselling genuine goods is not inherently illegal across most Latin American jurisdictions, so trademark and copyright takedowns rarely apply. The product is real. The breach is contractual.


‍


Unauthorized sellers source through distributor overstock, arbitrage buying, and return-channel goods, which keeps them supplied even when your distribution contracts are tight, a pattern also seen when dealing with[unauthorized sellers on Amazon](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/unauthorized-sellers-amazon) .


‍


Enforcement runs on separate tracks: pricing monitoring for MAP violations, listing policy infractions, and distribution agreement breaches. Seller identity on MercadoLibre is often thin, so tracing inventory leakage back to its source needs dedicated intelligence, not the reporting tool alone.


‍


‍


## Monitoring MercadoLibre at Scale Across 18 Countries


Treat MercadoLibre as a standing monitoring program, not a campaign. The Brand Protection Program runs real-time search across every MELI site, accepts bulk reports in a few clicks, and includes filters plus a seller audit tool to separate trustworthy sellers from suspicious ones.


‍


Set notifications on your brand keywords and sweep sale listings and store names for unauthorized use across all 18 country sites on a fixed cadence, much like the systematic approach used in[Temu IP infringement reporting](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/how-to-report-fake-products-on-temu) .


‍


Apply the same image-based and SKU-level detection described above to catch mark-stripped listings across all 18 storefronts. Sellers who omit your brand name from titles and descriptions never surface through standard queries, so pair keyword sweeps with image-based and SKU-level detection to catch listings that copy your product while stripping the mark.


‍


‍


## Escalation Paths Beyond the Brand Protection Program


When the BPP stops at listing removal, three escalation tracks remain. In Brazil, enforcement runs through civil lawsuits for infringement, administrative proceedings before INPI, and criminal actions for counterfeiting. Customs recordation intercepts goods at the border before they reach a listing.


‍


‍


National IP offices matter too. MercadoLibre has signed cooperation agreements with authorities including INDECOPI in Peru, which gives coordinated cases more weight. Similar cooperation frameworks exist on other major marketplaces.


‍


For high-volume infringers running multiple storefronts, none of this moves without physical evidence. A test purchase that documents an actual counterfeit is usually the prerequisite for any legal action beyond takedown, similar to what is required when you[file a counterfeit report on AliExpress](https://www.marqvision.com/blog/aliexpress-counterfeit) .


‍

## FAQ


### Do I need separate trademark registrations in Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina to file complaints through MercadoLibre's Brand Protection Program?


Yes: MercadoLibre's Brand Protection Program requires you to enroll rights separately for each country you want to report in, so a Mexican trademark registration gives you no standing to file complaints on the Argentine or Brazilian storefronts. Every Latin American jurisdiction runs on a first-to-file system, meaning you should register ahead of market entry and not wait until after, because a squatter who files before you can block enforcement entirely in that jurisdiction.


### How do counterfeit sellers on MercadoLibre evade keyword-based detection, and what does closing that gap actually require?


Sellers strip your brand name and trademark from listing titles and descriptions while copying your product images, specifications, and packaging, which means standard keyword sweeps never surface them. Closing that gap requires SKU-level comparison against genuine product data and image-based detection that catches listings replicating your visuals without using your mark. Without that layer, a meaningful share of infringing listings across MercadoLibre's 18-country footprint will never appear in a BPP search.


### What's the right enforcement path on MercadoLibre for gray market resellers vs. outright counterfeiters?


These two problems run on different tracks and should not be treated the same. For counterfeiters, the BPP takedown workflow applies directly: trademark or copyright evidence triggers listing removal and seller sanctions. For gray market resellers, the product is genuine, so IP-based takedowns rarely hold; enforcement runs through MAP violation monitoring, distribution agreement breaches, and seller identity tracing against reseller databases, not through the reporting tool. Conflating the two wastes enforcement resources and produces predictable complaint rejections.


### How do brands protect IP rights on MercadoLibre when a single enforcement program needs to cover Latin America's full geographic scope?


The practical constraint is registration coverage, not detection capability. MercadoLibre operates across 18 countries, and your complaints are only actionable in jurisdictions where you hold registered rights. Treat your trademark portfolio as a map that should track your distribution footprint: file in each country before you enter it, not after infringement appears. From there, a monitoring program that runs fixed-cadence sweeps across all country storefronts, pairs keyword searches with image-based detection, and routes gray market cases to a separate seller-intelligence workflow covers the scope the BPP alone cannot reach.


### When does brand protection on MercadoLibre require escalation beyond the Brand Protection Program itself?


The BPP stops at listing removal. When a high-volume infringer runs multiple storefronts and relists after each takedown, you need a physical test purchase to document the actual counterfeit before any civil lawsuit, criminal action, or customs recordation filing will move in Brazil, Mexico, or Argentina. National IP office cooperation agreements, such as MercadoLibre's coordination with INDECOPI in Peru, add weight to coordinated cases, but none of those escalation paths open without physical evidence tying a seller to confirmed counterfeit goods.


‍


‍

The Brand Protection Program is only as strong as the rights portfolio behind it and the monitoring cadence running on top of it. Registrations that lag your market entry, keyword-only sweeps, and one-off complaint bursts all leave gaps that experienced infringers know how to use.
